text: Jan Verhas painted portraits and genre scenes, often of the children of the Belgian bourgeoisie. His father Emmanuel, a painter who directed the academy in Dendermonde, gave him his first training, as he did his older brother Frans. From 1853 Verhas studied at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp under Nicaise de Keyser and Jan Antoon Verschaeren. Lawrence Alma-Tadema and Karel Ooms were fellow students, and the three stayed friends for life. In 1860 he finished his studies, spent a few months in Paris and took part in the Belgian Prix de Rome.

Jan Arends was the brother of the poet Roelof Arends and a pupil of J. Ponse. Born in Dordrecht in 1738, he worked for many years in Amsterdam and Middelburg, but he returned to Dordrecht and died there. He painted landscapes and marine subjects, he was well skilled in perspective, and he practised engraving. The collection here includes his views of an East India Company shipyard, dated 1779.

Maurice Greiffenhagen illustrated H. Rider Haggard's adventure books, starting with an edition of She in 1889, though he apparently disliked doing black-and-white work. He also illustrated the serialisations of Ayesha and The Holy Flower in the Windsor Magazine, and Edgar Wallace's Sanders of the River stories. He taught at the Glasgow School of Art for twenty years. His painting An Idyll, from 1891, inspired D. H. Lawrence's novel The White Peacock. He became a Royal Academician in 1922.

Michael Wolgemut ran a large workshop in Nuremberg, where Albrecht Dürer served an apprenticeship from 1486 to 1489. The workshop turned out big altarpieces and carved, painted wood retables. It also cut woodcuts from his designs, mostly as book illustrations for Nuremberg publishers. His woodcuts showed volume and shading to a much greater extent than before, and they were very often hand-coloured. Dürer built on this and went beyond it. Wolgemut died in 1519.

Pierre-Nicolas Brisset was apprenticed at eighteen in the workshop of Louis-Charles-Auguste Couder and later studied with François-Édouard Picot. A trip to Italy in 1835 inspired a series on historical subjects, monuments and ruins, notably the Ponte Nomentano. He won the Prix de Rome in 1840 and lived at the Villa Medici in Rome for four years. Later he assisted Picot with the frescoes at Saint-Vincent-de-Paul and painted murals of his own in several Paris churches. He died in 1890.

Jean-Baptiste Marie Pierre taught Nicolas-René Jollain at the Académie royale de peinture et de sculpture. Jollain painted a Danaë, which is now in a private collection. In 1768 he made two mythological scenes for the Palace of Versailles, Apollo mourning Hyacinth and Clytie changed into a sunflower. His Jesus among the Doctors is at the Palace of Fontainebleau. He lived from 1732 to 1804.

Pieter Mulier the Elder married in 1635, according to the RKD, and joined the Haarlem Guild of St. Luke three years later. He was known for Italianate landscapes and seascapes in the manner of Simon de Vlieger and Jan van Goyen. His pupils were his son Pieter Mulier II and Frans de Hulst. He was born in Haarlem around 1610 and died there in 1659. The collection here has his beach scenes and ships in heavy seas.

Giuseppe Camerata came from a family of painters and studied under Gregorio Lazzarini. He learned engraving from Giovanni Cattini. In 1751 he was invited to help engrave the plates for the Dresden Gallery, and there he was made principal engraver to the Court. He settled for a time in Munich. Later he became a professor at the Academy in Dresden, where he died in 1803. Sources are unsure whether he was born at Frascati or at Venice.

Pieter van Bleeck moved from The Hague to London in 1723 and worked there as a portrait painter and mezzotint engraver. He is especially known for theatrical subjects, among them Owen Swiny, Kitty Clive and Margaret Woffington. John Faber the Younger often engraved his paintings. His father, Richard van Bleeck, was a portrait painter too. In 1745 Pieter married Alice Cony, and the marriage bond understates his age. He died in 1764.

Willem Albracht painted portraits, interiors and landscapes. He studied at the Antwerp Academy and worked in the studio of Charles Verlat, and he travelled in Holland and Germany. In 1883 he was one of the founders of the Als ick Kan circle, which gathered young artists who wanted to put on exhibitions. In 1911 he had his own house built in eclectic style in the Zurenborg district of Antwerp, to a design by Hendrik Van Leemputten. The Museum of Fine Arts in Antwerp owns his picture of the old pharmacy of the charity office. He died in 1922.

Wojciech Stattler started out in mathematics and natural sciences, then switched to the drawing class of the School of Fine Arts in Kraków. He went on to Rome, where he studied at the Accademia di San Luca and privately with Vincenzo Camuccini and Bertel Thorvaldsen. From 1831 he taught as a professor in Kraków, and his pupil Jan Matejko became Poland's leading painter of historical events. In 1850 he returned to Rome. Stattler was a Polish Romantic painter of Swiss aristocratic ancestry, and he died in 1875.

Wu Zhen studied philosophy and swordsmanship, and soon after graduating he chose to become a painter. His paintings did not sell well, but close friends such as Wu Guan, Zhang Guan and Tao Zhongyi taught him how to paint. Many of his works are landscapes and paintings of bamboo. He sometimes added poems to them, which helped his calligraphy and poetry as well as his painting. He is counted among the Four Masters of the Yuan dynasty. He lived from 1280 to 1354.

Andrea Lilio came from Ancona and is also known as L'Anconitano. Pope Sixtus V employed him to decorate the Vatican library and the Scala Santa in San Giovanni Laterano, where he painted Moses striking the Rock. He is said to have been a pupil of Federico Barocci. Lilio made a popular niche for himself by painting allegories for aristocratic audiences, and he may have worked on the illustrations for Cesare Ripa's Iconologia. In a chapel of the Chiesa Nuova he painted the Archangel Michael driving fallen angels from Heaven. He died at Ascoli Piceno in 1642.

Cyril Kutlík founded the Serbian Drawing and Painting School in Belgrade in 1895, one of the first modern painting schools there. He was the third of thirteen children, and only five lived past ten. His father Bohdan was an evangelical priest and the editor of Czech and Slovak periodicals. Kutlík finished school in Hradec Králové. He is mostly known for Serbian folk-life motifs and for illustrating folk calendars. He died in 1900, at 31.

Before he painted, Christopher Pearse Cranch preached as a Unitarian minister, travelling from Providence to St. Louis. He was the youngest of 13 children of a chief judge in Washington, and his brother John became a painter too. Later he worked as a magazine editor, caricaturist, children's fantasy writer, poet and translator, as well as a landscape painter. He was close to the Transcendental Club. His daughter Caroline was a painter. He died in 1892.

The son of a Sheffield locksmith, Elisha Kirkall came to London around 1702 and found work in the book trade. He also studied drawing at the Great Queen Street Academy. Publishers liked the book ornaments he made as raised metal, and he became known for engravings on type metal that could be set up with letterpress as book illustrations. He used the mezzotint rocker tool to imitate chiaroscuro. Kirkall married twice and died at Whitefriars in December 1742, leaving a son, Charles.

Francesco Denanto, a woodcutter born in Savoy, worked in Rome in the 1520s. We know it from two notarial acts he signed there, one dated 6 January 1524. There is no evidence that he ever worked for Titian. One of his sets is a series of woodcuts on the life of Jesus, and he worked with Girolamo da Treviso, whose name is on two prints. Thierry Depaulis lists 21 prints by him, and 17 are kept in the British Museum. Michael Bury suggests he may have cut at least 50 woodblocks before he reached Rome.

From birth Ada Thilén's left eye was damaged, and she wore a glass eye for the rest of her life. She studied with Hjalmar Munsterhjelm at the Royal Swedish Academy of Arts in Stockholm and under Léon Bonnat and Jean-Léon Gérôme in Paris. She went on painting trips, including one to Brittany in 1886. Thilén painted landscapes and portraits in oils and also worked in pastel and watercolour. Her work stands for French realism of the 1880s, with some Italian influence. She died in 1933.

Gerhard Ludvig Lahde is remembered for hand-coloured, slightly caricatured prints of traditional costumes, made with Johannes Senn, and for pictures of big events such as the Copenhagen Fire of 1795 and the British bombardments of Copenhagen. He also made many portraits of prominent people. A tailor's son from Bremen, he trained as a goldsmith in Kiel. He then went to Copenhagen, entered the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts in 1787 and learned copperplate engraving from Johann Friderich Clemens. He died in 1833.

Giacomo Favretto painted genre scenes of his native Venice. The son of a carpenter, he spent many years in the family workshop. He was said to have been discovered in a stationer's shop, cutting out silhouettes to make a living. By thirty he had lost the sight of one eye. His genre painting at the Brera in Milan in 1873 attracted the attention of Camillo Boito, and in 1880 he won the Prince Umberto Prize there. He died in Venice in 1887.
